title: ICC Removes Its Chief Prosecutor. The Two Most Interested States Said Nothing.
subtitle: Russia and Israel each hold active ICC warrants and chose not to cover the court's first-ever removal of a chief prosecutor
body_md:
Eighty-two of the ICC's 125 member states voted Friday to remove Karim Khan as chief prosecutor, following allegations of sexual misconduct with a female staff member. The vote — the first-ever removal of an ICC chief prosecutor — drew broad factual consensus from 18 outlets across 13 countries, from Pakistan's Dawn to Canada's international press. The event was covered nearly identically across its factual content: the vote count, Khan's denial, the legal challenge he will pursue. The silence was more selective.

[AFP / France 24](https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20260724-icc-chief-prosecutor-karim-khan-dismissed-over-sexual-misconduct-allegations-sources-say) ran the wire baseline: "Member states of the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday voted to dismiss chief prosecutor Karim Khan following allegations of sexual misconduct." [Dawn](https://www.dawn.com/news/2018221/icc-members-vote-to-dismiss-karim-khan), the Pakistani daily whose country shares Khan's citizenship, reported that Khan "denies any wrongdoing and his lawyer said he will challenge his dismissal," adding that "82 of the court's 125 member states voted in favour of the prosecutor's removal."

The coverage's notable outlier on angle — not on facts — was [Malay Mail World](https://www.malaymail.com/news/world/2026/07/25/karim-khan-icc-prosecutor-who-sought-netanyahu-warrant-voted-out-over-malaysian-aides-sexual-misconduct-claims/228850), which headlined the dismissal by specifically naming the alleged victim's Malaysian nationality. The framing makes a regional identity claim on a story the outlet might otherwise have covered as a remote institutional matter. By foregrounding the Malaysian aide, Malay Mail turns a global legal proceeding into a story with a domestic protagonist — a legitimate editorial judgment, but one that no other outlet in the corpus made.

[The Hindu International](https://www.thehindu.com/news/international/fate-of-icc-chief-prosecutor-heads-to-unprecedented-vote-as-us-sanctions-keep-him-out-of-new-york/article71260792.ece) was the only outlet to report a structural irony that cuts directly to the ICC's institutional standing: US sanctions on Khan had prevented him from traveling to New York to attend the proceedings at which his fate was decided. The US is not a member of the ICC. Its sanctions — imposed separately from ICC proceedings — created the condition under which the chief prosecutor could not attend his own removal hearing. The Hindu International named this explicitly. No other outlet did.

Russia and Israel are both entirely absent from this corpus. Russia holds an active ICC arrest warrant against President Putin, issued in 2023. Israel has active arrest warrants against senior officials stemming from Gaza operations. Both countries have strong and immediate interests in the ICC's institutional functioning — and specifically in how effectively it can be paralyzed or delegitimized. The removal of a chief prosecutor under misconduct charges, followed by legal challenges, represents exactly the kind of institutional destabilization that reduces the practical threat of ICC action. Neither country's state media found it worth covering.

The coincidence of interests here is striking. The ICC is weakened by a vote that removes its chief prosecutor under contested circumstances. The two countries with the most to gain from ICC dysfunction declined to run the story. The coverage gap is itself a form of editorial signaling: neither Russia nor Israel wanted to draw attention to the ICC's continuing presence as an institution, even when that institution was visibly struggling.

Khan's legal challenge will take months. The ICC will need to appoint an interim or new prosecutor. How the court functions during that transition — and whether ongoing investigations, including those touching Israeli and Russian officials, continue at full capacity — is the question that 82 member states' vote has now opened.

The precedent question raised by Khan's removal is institutional rather than personal. The ICC has never removed a chief prosecutor before. The mechanism activated Friday exists in the Rome Statute but had been considered a theoretical safeguard rather than a practical one. Khan's planned legal challenge will test whether the removal was procedurally valid; the outcome will determine both whether Khan returns and what the threshold for future removals is. An institution whose founding prosecutor survived two decades of political pressure from non-member states — including the US and Russia — has now demonstrated that its internal democratic mechanism can remove its chief officer. Whether that makes the ICC stronger or more vulnerable to political campaigns against future prosecutors is not yet clear.
